articles.title: Democratic Socialist Principles in the Book of Acts
articles.author: DSA Religion and Socialism Working Group
articles.content_excerpt: The Mediterranean sun beat down upon the dusty limestone streets of Jerusalem, casting sharp shadows across a city fractured by imperial occupation, grinding poverty , and rigid social stratification. On the surface, the Roman peace—the Pax Romana —reigned supreme. But beneath that veneer lay a harsh economic reality: wealth was concentrated in the hands of a tiny elite, temple elites exacted heavy tributes, and the margins of society were choked with day laborers, widows, and orphans always on the brink of starvation. Yet, among a clandestine gathering of believers who had recently embraced the resurrected Galilean teacher, a radically different world was being born. articles.content_excerpt: By: Liam Noble BOSTON COMMON – On Saturday, October 3, anti-war protesters and left organizations rallied against the multiple simultaneous illegal wars prosecuted by the United States under the current regime — with a particular focus on the war in Iran. Protestors and local activists including Rabbi Greg Hersh and Tony Van Der Meer gave speeches condemning the loss of life caused by imperialist violence, especially in Latin America and West Asia. The atmosphere at the protest was one of shared outrage: against the illegal wars of aggression, the insanity of the US leadership, as well as over the deaths of and intentional targeting of civilians. articles.title: Who’s Your Uber Driver on the Phone to? Welcome to the Long, Long Diaspora Call
articles.author: Working Mass: The Massachusetts DSA Labor Outlet
articles.content_excerpt: The back of an Uber (Working Mass) By: Nesrine Malik This article was originally published by The Guardian on September 30, 2026. The question of the week is: “who are Uber drivers always talking to on the phone?” It’s one that regularly surfaces on Reddit threads and social media and even, on a couple of occasions, in the office. It’s not my question (I know who they are talking to), but I think the fact that many people are so baffled by it tells us a lot about the separate worlds we occupy. When you get a cab on a ride-hailing app, the chances that your driver will be on the phone is high. The conversation is almost always quiet, containing pauses so long that it often seems they are actually no longer on a call. articles.title: Tech Workers’ Leverage Over Employers Is Shifting
articles.author: JS Tan
articles.content_excerpt: Not long ago, tech companies courted their workers. Engineers were scarce enough that anyone who felt mistreated could quit and land somewhere else within weeks, so employers kept them around with generous perks and wide latitude on the job, and many firms took pains to look like the progressive institutions their staff expected them to be. That arrangement fell apart around 2022. Rising interest rates made executives far less willing to spend on their workforce, and many of them came to see their own employees’ activism as a problem to be crushed. Layoffs followed, aimed with notable precision at troublemakers, while the industry’s leaders bent the knee to Trump. articles.title: Mark Carney Isn’t the “Leader of the Free World.” Lula Is.
articles.author: Gerard Di Trolio
articles.content_excerpt: The headlines say it all: “Meet the New Leader of the Free World. No, It’s Not Donald Trump.” “ Canada’s Carney Claims Mantle of ‘Leader of the Free World.’” “How Mark Carney Became Leader of the Free World by Standing Up to Trump.” Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is not just incredibly popular at home but, increasingly, around the world. Now there is even talk of him winning the Nobel Peace Prize . It is a comforting fiction for those terrified by Donald Trump. But if any leader deserves such a title, it is not Canada’s ex-banker prime minister but Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. articles.author: Noah Gordon

articles.title: High School Protests Have French Establishment on the Ropes
articles.author: William Bouchardon
articles.content_excerpt: It only took a spark to set France ablaze. Protests broke out as the new school year had barely begun, as lycéens (high schoolers, aged roughly fifteen to eighteen) voiced their anger at what they see as neglect and contempt from the government. This deep-rooted discontent recalls earlier episodes. As the movement tries to spread to universities, the authorities’ only answer is repression, and accusations against La France Insoumise (LFI). The radical-left party wants to ride the wave of youth anger in its campaign for next spring’s presidential election, while its opponents hope the movement fizzles out as quickly as possible. articles.title: What Comes After Hyperpolitics?
articles.author: Anton Jäger
articles.content_excerpt: Before the end of this year, the United States will have broken two political records. According to the organizers’ own estimates, No Kings Day on March 28 was the largest single-day protest in recent American history. At the same time, no US president has so successfully enriched himself in office as Donald Trump has — 2026 is set to be the most lucrative year of his career so far. The concept of “hyperpolitics” is an attempt to explain these coincident phenomena. It describes a process of repoliticization without reinstitutionalization that has overtaken every layer of society in the wake of the 2008–9 crash. articles.title: Andy Burnham’s Labour Allows the Left to Breathe, a Little
articles.author: Harry Williams
articles.content_excerpt: “For too long, politics has not been working for people across Britain. We need to do better, and we will.” Such was Andy Burnham’s welcome to this year’s Labour Party conference. Gemma Bolton, a left-wing member of the party’s National Executive Committee, more simply summed up the change after years of purges, suspensions and rigged candidate selections: “Isn’t it nice you can breathe again?” This is roughly Burnham’s fortieth Labour conference, but his first as prime minister. His acclamation as party leader in July and this conference have been a break with the recent past under both Jeremy Corbyn and Keir Starmer, but in many ways represent a return to a much more traditional form of Labour politics. articles.title: Interest Rate Increases Are About Disciplining Labor
articles.author: Arthur MacEwan
articles.content_excerpt: Using its favored policy in the face of inflation, the Federal Reserve Board, under its new chairman, Kevin Warsh, pushed up short-term interest rates in September. This action may have some impact on the rate of inflation, but probably not much. Raising interest rates may curtail inflation under some circumstances, but the major factors bringing about the current, continuing inflation are unlikely to be much affected by the Fed’s recent interest rate increases. But those other factors are out of bounds: the Fed can’t alter them, and the current administration in Washington won’t. What Washington Has Done to Curtail Inflation With the emergence of economic instability in the early 1970s, President Richard Nixon imposed wage-price controls that limited how much wages and prices could rise.
